accuracy.evidence: Matches the Year 1 English programme of study (sit correctly at a table, hold a pencil comfortably and correctly, form lower-case letters in the correct direction starting in the right place). Grip guidance follows the occupational-therapy literature summarised by Schwellnus et al. 2012 (AJOT): the dynamic tripod is the usual teaching grip, quadrupod grips are equally fast and legible, and primitive fist grasps move the pencil with the whole forearm, which is why the lab's fist line wobbles. Letter starts follow common UK schemes: c, o, a, d start at the top of the round, l, n, t at the top, e in the middle; the wobble in the drawing step is a stated simplification of control, not a measurement.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips of four to six year olds: swinging feet or tucking them under the chair (predict options, challenge 'swing'/'chair', m6 adds the footstool fix), slumping (Pip's back, m9), the free hand idle in the lap (m1, challenge 'lap'), holding on the wooden tip or at the very top (hold zones with their own feedback, challenge 'tip'/'top', m5), a tight fist or flat stiff fingers (grip comparison, m2), squeezing too hard (challenge 'squeeze', m3), starting letters at the bottom, and over-applying 'start at the top' to e (the special e message, challenge 'etop', m4).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaggrip is built around posture and grip, not tracing: a side-view seated figure with three draggable fixes, a giant pencil with a draggable pinch whose drop position changes the sample line, and a free-drawing pad where the chosen grip changes the jitter of the learner's own line. Only the start-dot step relates to flagdigit, and it uses tap-the-dot with three candidate dots on letters rather than tracing digits; the 6-shingle distinctness gate passes.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner act and see the consequence: Pip only becomes steady after feet, back and other hand are fixed; dropping the pinch high, mid, on the paint or on the wood draws a wobbly, bumpy, smooth or smudged hidden line with a short reason; drawing with fist, flat fingers and pinch shows the smooth line appear only with the pinch (the task needs at least two grips tried); tapping a start dot animates the letter being written from that point, so the direction is seen, and Your turn includes e as the exception.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions are committed before acting and are revealed against the result: where the feet go, where to hold the pencil, which grip draws the best line, and where most letters start. Each wrong option is a genuine child belief (swinging feet, holding on the tip, a tight fist, starting at the bottom), and the completion message names the prediction and explains why the right answer works.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating challenge kinds (feet, pencil spot, grip, other hand, where l starts, where e starts, how tight) with rotated answer order. Every wrong answer gets its own short reason and fix, for example 'A fist moves the whole arm, so the line wobbles. Pinch it instead.' and 'Most letters start at the top, but e starts in the middle.'; correct answers build a star streak, and Another gives a new question.

readability.evidence: Kid text and every lab string use short sentences and everyday words for ages four to six (feet flat, sit tall, pinch, paint, wood, gently like a baby bird); button labels are two to five words; challenge answers are short phrases. Adult text holds the detail (tripod, quadrupod, 2 cm from the tip, left-handed tilt) so the child-facing layer stays simple enough to read aloud together.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a concrete instruction or reason: the curriculum expectation, the set-up checklist with the footstool fix, the specific mistakes with their effects, left-handed advice, and practical practice ideas (broken crayons, pegs, saying the start aloud) with a clear point to talk to the teacher. Items test exactly what the lab practised; the content gate passes its filler and similarity checks.

mobile.evidence: Walked through at 375 px on a touch-emulated phone: drag handles have 40 px hit radii, the pinch has a 44 px radius, letter dots are at least 14 px drawn with a 26 px hit zone, grip cards span a third of the width, status labels sit right-aligned clear of the figure, the letter box is centred in the taller narrow canvas, and every control has a large button twin; no button overflows or is under 32 px tall, and synthetic touch drags fixed feet, hand and back, placed the pinch in all zones and drew lines.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (three fix buttons, four hold spots, three grips plus Draw a line and Clear, named start dots per letter), the canvas aria-label is kept in sync with a plain description of the scene and the last result, challenge feedback is in a polite live region, colour is never the only cue (ticks and circles on the checklist, text reasons for every zone), reduced motion skips animation timing, and axe passes in light and dark themes on desktop and phone.
